partners.mechanism_chain: BTK (HGNC:1037) —DISRUPTS→ BTK signaling pathway (WP:WP466); BTK signaling pathway (WP:WP466) —LEADS_TO→ Growth hormone deficiency (HP:0000824); BTK signaling pathway (WP:WP466) —LEADS_TO→ Immunodeficiency (HP:0011421); NCKAP1L (HGNC:29801) —LEADS_TO→ Isolated growth hormone deficiency type III (MONDO:0010615); BTK (HGNC:1037) —LEADS_TO→ Immunodeficiency 72 with autoinflammation (MONDO:0033551). Loss-of-function mutations in BTK disrupt the BTK signaling pathway, which can lead to both immunodeficiency and, in some contexts, growth hormone deficiency. ### CANDIDATE DETAIL
#### 1. Bruton-type agammaglobulinemia  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.785)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-2029482, Reactome:R-HSA-2871809, Reactome:R-HSA-416476, Reactome:R-HSA-5603041, Reactome:R-HSA-9664422)

**Proposed mechanism:** BTK (HGNC:1133) —DISRUPTS→ B-cell development and signaling (GO:0002393); B-cell development and signaling (GO:0002393) —LEADS_TO→ Agammaglobulinemia (HP:0004324); BTK (HGNC:1133) —DISRUPTS→ Pituitary somatotroph development and function (GO:0048440); Pituitary somatotroph development and function (GO:0048440) —LEADS_TO→ Growth hormone deficiency (HP:0000702); Growth hormone deficiency (HP:0000702) —LEADS_TO→ Short stature (HP:0004303). Loss-of-function mutations in BTK disrupt B-cell development, leading to agammaglobulinemia. Concurrently, BTK also plays a role in pituitary somatotroph development and function, and its disruption leads to growth hormone deficiency, manifesting as short stature.

**How to falsify it:** The identification of pathogenic variants in BTK that are exclusively associated with either agammaglobulinemia or growth hormone deficiency, without any overlap, would falsify this hypothesis. Additionally, if genetic studies reveal distinct, non-BTK related causal genes for one of the diseases that do not converge on any shared downstream pathways, this would also serve as a falsification condition. _(variant: Identification of common benign variants in BTK in individuals with isolated growth hormone deficiency type III.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the dual role of BTK in both immune and endocrine systems could lead to novel therapeutic strategies. For instance, targeting BTK signaling might offer a way to modulate growth hormone secretion in patients with isolated growth hormone deficiency type III, or conversely, understanding growth hormone's role in immunity might inform treatment for Bruton's agammaglobulinemia.

Loss-of-function mutations in BTK disrupt B cell receptor signaling, leading to immunodeficiency and systemic inflammation (Disease B). Concurrently, BTK dysfunction also impacts growth hormone synthesis and secretion pathways, resulting in short stature (Disease A).

**How to falsify it:** Identification of pathogenic variants in BTK with a clear loss-of-function effect in patients with isolated growth hormone deficiency type III and immunodeficiency 82 with systemic inflammation would support this hypothesis. Conversely, if variants in BTK are found to be benign or absent in affected individuals of either disease cohort, or if a distinct causal gene is identified for one of the diseases, this hypothesis would be falsified. _(variant: gnomad v2.1.1 allele frequency > 0.001 for proposed pathogenic variants in BTK)_

Loss-of-function mutations in BTK disrupt the BTK signaling pathway, which can lead to both immunodeficiency and, in some contexts, growth hormone deficiency. **How to falsify it:** If genetic analysis reveals that the causal variants for isolated growth hormone deficiency type III (MONDO:0010615) are exclusively in NCKAP1L and do not affect BTK or its downstream signaling, and that the causal variants for immunodeficiency 72 with autoinflammation (MONDO:0033551) are exclusively in BTK and do not have any pleiotropic effects on pituitary development, this hypothesis would be falsified. _(variant: rs121918457 (a common variant in BTK))_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of BTK in both immune function and pituitary development could lead to novel therapeutic strategies for growth hormone deficiency, potentially by modulating BTK signaling. It also highlights the importance of considering pleiotropic effects of genes involved in complex developmental disorders.
